doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Billie Holiday, band members and singers
title: First overdubbing: playing clarinet to a recorded band on Love for Sale
summary: A dental problem led him to add his part later through earphones to a recorded 44-piece band, an early dubbing.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So you didn’t actually tour with Mel Tormé?

Oh, no no. That was studio work. Studio orchestras. Matter of fact, the first time an instrument was dubbed was in those sessions, on Love For Sale. I had to have some dental work done on the front of my mouth. I didn’t know it, but there was a tooth that had to be recapped. I didn’t know that at the time. The band was called for a date, and there were I think 44 men in the studio. Big string section. I had to show up, and either pay the 44 men . . . So I finally said to one of the control men, “Is there any way we could make my recording, stick it in over this some way, later?” The guy said, “We’ve never done it, but we could try it.”
This is before tape, is it?
I’m not sure we had tape or not. I don’t know what they did.
1940s. Early 1940s. [recording engineer:] They had a tape machine in the ’40s, I think.
We recorded the tunes. Love For Sale and whatever it was . . .

. . . and I came at a later date and played with the earphones. So it must have been tape. But that was a brand new idea. I thought it was a hell of an idea, because then I could think of what I was doing. Never mind what the band was doing. That was done. Play it over a few times and then play it like I was listening to a band and playing my part.
That was the start of something, wasn’t it?
Yeah. God. Now you can make a career out of that.
